frase_gancho.texto: Maximilian called this palace Miravalle and chose to live in the rooms that face east, toward the city and the volcanoes.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue the tour to the rooms of President Porfirio Díaz and his wife Carmen, in a very different Castle.

guion_corto.texto: Miravalle. That is what Maximilian called his palace at Chapultepec, and the name explains itself: a place to look out over the valley. The museum explains that the emperors chose the ground-floor rooms that face east. From there you can see the capital, Lake Texcoco and the volcanoes. That is why they had a panoramic terrace built. Maximilian was an archduke of Austria and had been a naval officer. Before coming to Mexico he built Miramar Castle, in Trieste. Between eighteen sixty-four and eighteen sixty-seven he left gardens and a terrace on this hill. He also left the layout of an avenue that is now the Paseo de la Reforma.

guion_largo.texto:
Ferdinand Maximilian Joseph was the second son of Prince Franz Karl of Austria. His family, the Habsburgs, had a motto in Latin: Austria est imperare orbi universo, that is, it falls to Austria to rule the entire world. He was a naval officer and governor general of Lombardy and Venetia. In Trieste, facing the Adriatic Sea, he had Miramar Castle built, and that fondness for places with a view went with him to Mexico.

He accepted the crown of Mexico on the tenth of April, eighteen sixty-four, in that same Miramar Castle. He arrived at Veracruz in late May, aboard the frigate Novara, he at thirty-one years old and Carlota at twenty-four. He was the first descendant of the Catholic Monarchs to cross the Atlantic and set foot on American soil. In June he was in the capital. The country then had two governments: the Empire, sustained by the French army, and the Republic of [Benito Juárez](chap_07_carruaje_juarez), which did not recognize it. In that deeply divided climate, they chose Chapultepec.

The Mexican architect Ramón Rodríguez Arangoity turned the building into a palace. The Austrian botanist Wilhelm Knechtel redesigned the gardens, although Carlota credited the result more to Maximilian’s own hand. The sovereigns chose the ground-floor rooms facing east, and that is why they built the panoramic terrace. The museum also notes that Maximilian called his palace Miravalle and that he used those terraces to read and write. From the Castle, a great avenue also ran out, inspired by the Ringstrasse in Vienna, linking the palace with the center of the city. Today it is the Paseo de la Reforma, and you can picture it from the [east terrace](chap_26_terraza_oriente_reforma).

The conservatives who had backed him expected an emperor made to measure, and they got a surprise. According to the Secretaría de Educación Pública, Maximilian upheld the Reform Laws and declared religious tolerance. He also allowed the sale of church properties and returned lands to Indigenous communities. The conservatives felt betrayed, although some liberals agreed to collaborate with the Empire.

Then came the fall. In eighteen sixty-six, pressure from Prussia in Europe and from the United States in America led Napoleon the Third to withdraw his troops and cut off financing. Without them, the Empire grew weak. At the end of eighteen sixty-six, on leaving Mexico City, Maximilian ordered his palaces dismantled, Chapultepec among them. He went to Querétaro, where he was captured in May of eighteen sixty-seven. On the nineteenth of June he was executed by firing squad at the Cerro de las Campanas, together with Generals Miguel Miramón and Tomás Mejía.

There is an account from a witness. The Hungarian physician Ede Szenger wrote in eighteen seventy-six about that day, and said he had witnessed it. According to him, Maximilian gave an ounce of gold to each soldier of the firing squad and bared his chest before the volley. It is one person’s recollection, not an official document, and it should be read with that caution.

In this Alcázar, the museum associates with Maximilian a brass bed that remained in the Castle after his death. And if you want to see the carriage that Maximilian and Carlota used, and that Juárez later used, the museum mentions it in the [Carriage Hall](chap_12_sala_carruajes). From there the story passes to another ruler, very different, who also made this hill his summer home: Porfirio Díaz.

texto: Look for the windows or the terrace that face east, the direction the emperors chose
Look for the name Miravalle on a wall label
If you see a brass bed, remember that the museum associates it with Maximilian

texto.Work on the Alcázar: architect Ramón Rodríguez Arangoity; gardens by the botanist Wilhelm Knechtel
texto.End: executed by firing squad in Querétaro on June 19, 1867

texto.pregunta: Myth: Maximilian was a conservative emperor who gave power and property back to the Church.
texto.respuesta: Reality: according to the Secretaría de Educación Pública, he upheld the Reform Laws, allowed the sale of church properties and declared religious tolerance, and that is why the conservatives felt betrayed.
